papers.title: Buessecker et al. 2019: chemical nitrous oxide production from nitrite in tropical peat (no freezing, one soil, no nitric oxide)
Green et al. 2022: nitrous oxide sources in soil (did not separate chemical from biological production or test subzero temperatures)

No soil measurement was found, and Wertz et al. 2018 saw nitrite accumulate at -2 C in live soil, which argues against fast net loss. Soil buffering and the eutectic cut-off make the direction uncertain.

why: A strong mechanism in the lab that nobody seems to have tested in soil, and a clean experiment can settle it, but the one soil result points the other way.
title: Freezing speeds the chemical loss of nitrite and nitrous oxide in soil

A paper on the copper chaperone for nitrous oxide reductase: below 0.5 uM copper a mutant strain accumulated up to about 4 mM nitrous oxide (read through a summary, not in full)
A paper describing the copper-sulfur cluster at the nitrous oxide reductase active site (read through a summary, not in full)

why: A clean, testable sulfate-by-copper experiment on a real enzyme mechanism, but the author checked the sources only through summaries and iron in porewater could remove the effect.
title: Sulfate and copper shortage raise nitrous oxide release in wetlands

Renkl et al. 2026: a modelled heatwave-intensified atmospheric river with 19-55% more California rain (one event, no runoff or carbon)
Clark et al. 2022: extreme rainstorms drive exceptional organic carbon export from Puerto Rico rivers (summary page read)

why: Two well-documented effects nobody has joined, with data that already exist, but heavier rain may not carry more carbon per millimetre and the heatwave result comes from a single study.
title: Marine heatwaves raise river carbon export during storms

Bommarco et al. 2012: oilseed rape and pollination, +18% seed weight per plant (repository page; yield and quality only)

Only 5 papers mention pollination with nitrogen leaching, and none are on point by title.

why: A link between farm ecology and the nitrogen cycle that nobody seems to have measured, with a clear field design, but the leaching effect is small and crops can compensate.
title: Poor pollination leaves more nitrogen in the field and raises leaching

A study of the nitrous oxide reductase gene in Pseudomonas stutzeri: its transcription fell above 0.5 mM copper
A basalt-soil study: soils average 43.9 mg/kg copper, attributed to the basalt parent material

web.text: Copper is established as a requirement of the enzyme that turns nitrous oxide into nitrogen, and basalt soils are copper-rich. Bedrock also changes pH and carbon, which could swamp a copper effect.

why: A clean field comparison built on a proven enzyme mechanism, but bedrock changes several things at once and the copper doses tested so far were additions, not natural levels.
title: Copper-rich bedrock lowers nitrous oxide release from soil

Gauci et al. 2004: sulfur pollution suppresses the wetland methane source (opening of the abstract only)

why: Strength: mechanism and sign are supported by field and modelling work and the lab test is easy; risk: bare-soil albedo is rarely the exposed surface in real land use, so real-world offset is soil- and cover-dependent.

untested: Isotope tracing (33P or 15N) of nutrient delivery through hyphae to plants across snow-manipulation plots, and the generality beyond one subalpine meadow and AMF, are not shown; the preprint infers nutrient effects from soil pools. It also is not peer reviewed.

papers.title: Preprint: experimentally advanced snowmelt in a subalpine meadow caused plant greening to start early and cut extraradical AM hyphal production, with smaller available N and P pools; one site, not yet peer reviewed, nutrient transfer not traced

Hubbard Brook 29-month root-exclusion and ingrowth cores along a snow-depth gradient: grouped AM and EM abundance unaffected by snow depth, ericoid fungi rose with snow, some orders responded; single sampling, no hyphal timing or nutrient transfer

web.text: A recent early-snowmelt experiment reports plant-fungal asynchrony with reduced hyphal production and smaller nutrient pools, which closely matches the prediction. A forest snowpack-decline study found little change in grouped mycorrhizal abundance, so the effect may vary by system and fungal group.

why: Strength: a direct early-snowmelt experiment already shows the predicted mismatch; risk: forest and Arctic snow studies show mixed fungal responses and nutrient delivery has not been traced.

untested: Multi-year (3-5 year) persistence of the abundance-up, richness-down shift and its link to measured C and N turnover (CUE, N mineralisation) has not been shown; follow-ups were 7 months or less, and the copiotroph shift was inferred from taxa rather than traits or rates.

papers.title: Hurricane Otto, Costa Rica: soil sampled 3 months before and 7 months after; microbial biomass up, genus richness down, shift to dominant functional-group genera; single storm, short horizon, no turnover rates

Luquillo Canopy Trimming Experiment: green debris deposition and canopy opening decoupled; soil microbial community changed pre vs post but did not separate by treatment, effects possibly missed or masked; bacterial richness showed a positive response to some treatment

web.text: A Costa Rica study found the predicted abundance increase and richness decrease after a hurricane, but the best controlled experiment (Luquillo canopy trimming) found treatment effects were masked by strong background variation and resilience. Multi-year persistence and process-rate consequences remain unmeasured.

why: Strength: an observational precedent and an existing manipulation platform make it testable; risk: experimental work shows microbial resilience, so lasting copiotroph shifts and rate changes are uncertain.

untested: No test with trees in seasonally dry forest or shrubland that measures protease activity and gross N mineralization with lift blocked by trenching or shading and deuterium-labelled deep water; existing work is sagebrush with augmented deep water and grass in pots, with no protease assays.

papers.title: Sagebrush field experiment: adding deep water raised lift, soil respiration and 15N cycling in surface soil and N uptake into inflorescences; shrub not tree, no protease assay or blocked-lift control
Grass in two-layer pots with lift blocked by 24 h light: decomposition and uptake higher with lift, mixed NH4/NO3 signs; greenhouse, grass, no protease or gross mineralization by pool dilution
Hydraulic redistribution may stimulate decomposition: diel drying-rewetting of root litter in a desert system; decomposition only, not enzymes or N rates

web.text: Field and pot experiments show hydraulic lift raises topsoil decomposition and N cycling in sagebrush and grass. The specific claim for trees, protease activity and gross mineralization with a blocked-lift contrast, and the 20-100% size, are untested.

links.label: Hydraulic lift and N cycling in grass, 2012

why: Strength: a sagebrush field study already shows more surface N cycling with lift; risk: trenching and root exclusion confound lift with root death and competition, and lift in trees may be too small to matter.

untested: A clean forested-versus-sparse basin contrast of runoff ratio against CO2 with precipitation, temperature, land use and leaf area as covariates, backed by FACE sap-flow checks, is not settled; the global catchment attribution found near-zero median CO2 effect, so the predicted runoff-ratio rise is not detected.

papers.title: Global climate model with a vegetation component: physiological forcing from doubled CO2 raised simulated global runoff by about 6%; a model projection, not an observed basin trend

Catchment-scale attribution across 1116 unimpacted catchments, 1981-2020, constrained by observed streamflow: median direct CO2 contribution approached zero; the opposite of a detectable decades-long runoff-ratio rise

web.text: Models predict higher runoff from CO2-driven stomatal closure, but observation-constrained catchment analyses find the net effect is close to zero because greater leaf area and growth offset the lower conductance. Other work argues the effect depends on aridity, so the sign can differ by climate.

links.label: Direct CO2 effect on streamflow, Nat Commun 2024

why: Strength: well-defined regression and strong mechanistic basis; risk: observation-based attribution already finds a near-zero effect, with leaf-area greening and climate offsets cancelling stomatal closure.

untested: The size and persistence of the effect for atmospheric deposition specifically (as opposed to fertilizer additions) at chronic low doses, and in which soils the response saturates or declines, are less clear; the core N-raises-phosphatase link is already established.

papers.title: Meta-analysis of 34 studies: N fertilization enhanced phosphatase activity from tropics to extra-tropics, in roots and bulk soil, while P fertilization suppressed it; mostly fertilizer, not deposition gradients
Letter on long-term N addition: N stimulation of soil phosphatase appears to decline progressively with years of N addition, citing a long-term chaparral-type record; indicates the effect can fade
7-year simulated N deposition in calcareous grassland raised root-surface phosphomonoesterase activity in three plant functional types; plant roots not bulk soil

web.text: A multi-biome meta-analysis finds N addition raises phosphatase activity, and deposition-simulation experiments show the same in plant roots. Evidence that the stimulation can fade with decades of N addition means the direction holds but the long-term size is uncertain.

links.label: Deposition and root phosphatase, calcareous grassland

why: Strength: a meta-analysis across biomes already shows the predicted direction; risk: little novelty, and long-term N saturation can erase the effect.

untested: Validation against deep hydrographic sections and abyssal temperature trends with modern flux maps and eddy-resolving or multi-model comparisons is incomplete; existing numbers come from one global model configuration and the Arctic deep-warming signal exceeds what geothermal heating explains.

papers.title: Ocean model with no, uniform and spatially varying geothermal heat flux: with strong mixing the AABW cell strengthened about 15% (2.5 Sv), deep North Pacific warmed up to 0.3 C and Southern Ocean poleward heat transport rose about 10%; single model, climatological data

Deep Arctic Ocean warming observed at 0.020 C/decade exceeds what geothermal heating explains; attributes the excess to heat transferred from the deep Atlantic; does not test global overturning with and without geothermal flux
Coupled climate model preprint: geothermal heating weakens deep stratification and strengthens AABW and deepens the AMOC in the Last Glacial Maximum, with a different sea-ice response today; preprint

web.text: Emile-Geay and Madec ran ocean model pairs with and without spatially varying geothermal heat flux and reported about a 15% stronger AABW cell and about 10% more Southern Ocean poleward heat transport, almost exactly the stated estimate. What remains is observational validation and robustness across models.

why: Strength: the stated 10-15% AABW and heat-transport estimates match a published model result; risk: results depend on the mixing parameterization, and little new remains beyond observational validation.

untested: No study found pairing debris-rich and debris-poor glacier catchments and linking dust grain size and mineralogy to the weathering or erosion rate of surrounding rock; existing work shows dust and local moraine sources matter at single glaciers but does not test the weathering-rate dependence or the 1-9 W/m2 range.

papers.title: Vadret da Morteratsch: summer albedo fell 0.32 to 0.15 after 2003 from mineral and biogenic dust, ~3.5 m extra ice loss over 2003-06 (equal to +1.7 K air temperature); moraine dust named as an important feedback; one glacier, no weathering-rate link
Argentiere Glacier model: Saharan dust cut annual mass balance by 0.31-0.45 m w.e. and accounted for about 8-16% of summer melt; long-range dust, modelled, no catchment debris or weathering analysis

web.text: Dust on glaciers, including dust from exposed moraines and bedrock, lowers albedo and speeds melt, with effects ranging from small to large by site and a tropical Andes study finding under 1% reflectivity loss. The specific dependence on weathering intensity of the surrounding catchment is not tested.

why: Strength: dust-darkening of glaciers is documented, including from local moraines; risk: dust amount depends on wind, source exposure and snow cover more than on weathering rate, so the proposed causal link may be weak or confounded.

untested: No study found regressing dust immersion-freezing temperature against a weathering index (such as CIA) with measured feldspar content; existing work characterises pure feldspars and shows feldspar dominates dust ice nucleation, not how source-soil weathering changes it. Biological and organic ice nucleators in soil dust can mask feldspar at warmer temperatures.

papers.title: Droplet-freezing assays: feldspar, especially K-feldspar, dominates ice nucleation by mineral dust at mixed-phase conditions despite being a minor component, clays unimportant; did not vary source weathering intensity

Survey of 15 feldspars: K-rich alkali feldspars usually nucleate ice better than Ca-bearing plagioclase, large within-group variability, some activity loss when aged in water (about 2 C for hyper-active K-feldspar over 16 months); pure minerals, not weathered soil dusts
Perthite feldspar powders: onset -2 to -4 C and site populations tied to exsolution and microcline structure; industrial powders, no weathering gradient

web.text: Feldspar content and structure control mineral-dust ice nucleation, and ageing in water lowers activity somewhat, so weathering that removes K-feldspar should reduce activity. I found no measurement along a weathering-intensity gradient, and the size of a few degrees C shift is untested.

why: Strength: a clean field-to-lab gradient test with XRD and freezing assays; risk: soil dust also carries organic and biological ice nucleators, and clays or surface coatings could shift activity independently of feldspar content.

untested: Direct 14C-dead CO2 measurements in soil gas and river water along an erosion-rate gradient on shale, with microbial-inhibitor incubations, are only partly done; the heat released by rock organic carbon respiration is not measured or shown to matter.

papers.title: Taiwan Central Range soils: on average 67% of bedrock OCpetro oxidised in soils, CO2 emission 6.1-18.6 t C/km2/yr rising with erosion rate; microbial mediation shown by lipid biomarkers and isotopes; did not use inhibitors or measure heat

Rhenium-based global catchment extrapolation: rock organic carbon oxidation releases CO2 rivalling or exceeding silicate weathering drawdown, hotspots in uplifted fine-grained sedimentary mountains; flux estimate from rhenium, not direct respiration

web.text: Rhenium and biomarker work shows rock organic carbon is oxidised in soils and rivers with fluxes that rise with erosion rate, and that oxidation is microbially mediated. The global flux estimate and Taiwan share match the stated figures in kind, while respiration heat and inhibitor-controlled incubations are not reported.

why: Strength: the erosion-rate dependence and microbial mediation are published and the proposed test is established practice; risk: the heat-release claim is trivial and unmeasurable in practice, and the CO2 flux has chemical (abiotic) oxidation as a competing pathway.

untested: A matched-hillslope comparison with different weathering depth and fracture density at equal rainfall, scaling dry-season transpiration share (the 10-30% of annual rainfall estimate) with fracture density and weathering depth, is not found; existing work shows bedrock water use is widespread but not how it scales across sites.

papers.title: Continental-US estimate of bedrock-water contribution to transpiration: woody plants routinely access rock moisture, not only in drought; lower-bound estimate from datasets, no matched-hillslope or fracture-density scaling
Direct observation of rock moisture in a weathered-bedrock hillslope: weathered zone tens of metres thick stores water that plants draw down; one site, no cross-site comparison with unfractured rock
Review of bedrock as a tree water reservoir under drought: notes uncertainty on pathways and efficiency of rock-root exchange; synthesis not a matched test

web.text: Several studies show trees draw on water stored in weathered or fractured bedrock, especially in dry seasons, and that this is widespread. The dose-response with fracture density and the specific transpiration share are not established.

why: Strength: bedrock water use by trees is well documented and the proposed measurements are established; risk: confounding by rooting depth, species and climate makes a clean matched-site contrast hard, and thick weathered rock can also lower runoff rather than raise transpiration.

untested: Whether films of surfactant (surface-active molecules) that build up during lake algal blooms cut the gas transfer velocity for CO2 and methane by 20-50% at the same wind speed, so that wind-based models overestimate bloom-period gas release by roughly 1.3-2 times. The effect is established at sea; the lake version is untested.

papers.title: Mustaffa et al. 2020: gas transfer 23% lower above 200 ug Teq/L surfactant and 62% lower in slicks, including a Trichodesmium bloom (all marine)
Pereira et al. 2016: lab tank with coastal water showed 14-51% suppression of gas transfer (marine; no blooms or freshwater)
Khan et al. 2026, Lake Stechlin: calls surfactant suppression plausible but untested (no surfactant measurements)
Karnatz et al. 2026: surfactants rise under cyanobacteria-dominated conditions at sea (no gas transfer measured)

web.text: Surfactant films are well shown to slow gas exchange at sea, and blooms raise surfactants. No study measured it in lakes: only 8 papers combine microlayer, gas transfer and film terms, and none are on topic. A 2021 cruise analysis reportedly found no chlorophyll-surfactant link, and bloom pH and CO2 drawdown change flux separately from the transfer velocity.

why: A proven marine effect applied to lakes with standard measurements, but it is mostly an extension of known work and bloom chemistry can confound the flux.
title: Algal bloom films slow gas exchange in lakes

untested: Whether, over rock rich in oxidizing iron-bearing minerals (biotite granite, quartz diorite, gneiss), the depth to which trees draw seasonal rock moisture follows the depth of the biotite-oxidation and fracture front, and is shallower over biotite-poor rock. No study measured both together.

papers.title: Holbrook et al. 2019: a 65 m borehole shows iron loss and fractured, expanded biotite from about 38 m, with fracture density rising from about 4% to 16% (no roots or moisture measured)
Napieralski et al. 2019: iron-oxidizing bacteria oxidize biotite iron in lab incubations of crushed rock (no fracturing, flow or roots)
Rempe and Dietrich 2018: rock moisture is about 4.7 times soil moisture, with roots seen to 16 m (rock types not compared)
Crutchfield-Peters et al. 2025: trees draw bedrock water to about 7 m (no mineral oxidation measured)

web.text: Each side is documented: biotite oxidation fractures rock, and trees use water stored in weathered rock. A search for biotite together with rock moisture found nothing. Counter-evidence: rock moisture also sits in older tectonic fractures and clay-rich rock, and iron loss may be a result of water flowing along fractures, not their cause.

why: A drilling and moisture comparison on two rock types would settle it, but the author did not read the few papers that overlap and the cause could run the other way.
title: How deep iron minerals have oxidized sets how deep trees draw rock water
Forest spore ice nuclei glaciate clouds warmer than ocean air
untested: No study links wet-night spore INP enhancement over forest to warmer cloud-top glaciation temperature or a larger ice-rain share versus dust-free ocean air; the 10x and 2-5 C magnitudes are untested and confounded by aerosol, dynamics and cloud-top height.

papers.title: Bioaerosols (fluorescent biological particles) were the main INP source at -12 to -20 C in coastal California; tested INP speciation and model skill, not cloud-phase response or rain ice fraction
Convective-storm study in Colorado: rain raised fungal spore counts and measured INPs alongside; did not link to cloud-top phase or compare forest vs ocean
Satellite T* (mixed-phase transition temperature) shifts with snow/sea-ice cover, showing surface INP sources influence cloud phase at high latitudes; did not look at forest or biological INPs
Eastern Mediterranean orographic clouds: INPs show diurnal cycle driven by fluorescent bioaerosol; no forest-versus-ocean glaciation contrast

web.text: Biological INPs dominate the -12 to -20 C range in several continental and coastal settings, rain and humid nights raise fungal spore and INP loads, and satellite work shows surface INP sources can shift cloud-phase transition temperature. The specific chain from spore INPs to warmer cloud-top glaciation over forest and a higher ice-rain share has not been measured, and cloud-top phase is strongly affected by updraft strength and other aerosol.

why: Strength: each link (spore INPs, rain enhancement, INP control of phase) has support; risk: the combined 10x and 2-5 C claims are large and confounded by dynamics, so a clean forest-versus-ocean test is hard.

title: Deforestation raises river silica and favours coastal diatoms
untested: The catchment half (more dissolved silica after clearing) has been measured at Hubbard Brook; what is untested is whether the extra silica raises Si:N at river mouths and shifts coastal phytoplankton toward diatoms, and whether this holds for cropland conversion, where fertiliser N and dams may reverse it.

papers.title: Hubbard Brook clear-cut raised stream dissolved silicate loss (Conley et al.); did not follow silica downstream to coastal phytoplankton (abstract not opened in full, record page redirected to Wiley)
Six decades at Hubbard Brook: deforested catchment W5 showed sustained rises in streamwater pH, Ca and SiO2 export for nearly four decades; no coastal or diatom test
GlASS database: 421 rivers with DSi, N, P and watershed traits, built to test land cover effects on Si and stoichiometry; a data source, not a test of the diatom prediction
Rhine and Yangtze model: Yangtze Si export fell as damming and cropland conversion occurred, the opposite sign to the cropland branch of the prediction

web.text: Experimental deforestation at Hubbard Brook increases dissolved silica export for decades, which supports the catchment half. Basin-scale studies show that damming and cropland conversion can instead lower Si delivery, and N and P enrichment usually lowers Si:N, so the coastal diatom shift is not established and may be swamped by nutrients and reservoirs.

why: Strength: the silica rise after clear-cutting is documented and GlASS data exist; risk: the downstream diatom signal is tiny against N, P and dam effects and cropland conversion may reduce Si export.

title: Virus-collapsed blooms emit sea spray with more ice nuclei
untested: No study has infected a host culture with its virus, aerosolised it and compared INP per unit sea salt with the growth phase, and no field work links INP or supercooled-liquid loss to bloom age or free-virus counts.

papers.title: Two-bloom mesocosm: ice-nucleating sea spray rose only during the first (growth-phase) bloom, not in the second; tracked bloom stage but not viral lysis, and points the opposite way for the collapse phase
Planktonic exudates (proteins and polysaccharides) act as sea-spray ice-nucleating agents, fitted with a freezing model; did not compare healthy vs virus-infected cells
Polysaccharides from aquatic eukaryotes explain about 44 percent of marine INPs at -15 to -20 C in a model; no viral infection treatment
Virus-infected phytoplankton cultures produce aerosolised organic matter of different molar mass and hygroscopicity; measured CCN activity, not ice nucleation

web.text: Marine INPs come largely from microbial exudates and polysaccharides, and viral lysis releases such organic matter, so a link is plausible. The one bloom mesocosm that tracked INPs saw the increase during growth, not decline, and Southern Ocean INP levels are generally low, so a 3x enhancement in the collapse phase and a cloud-phase signal are speculative.

links.label: Virus infection and aerosol CCN activity

why: Strength: a clean mesocosm test with infected vs control cultures is feasible; risk: existing bloom data show INPs peaking in growth, and the satellite cloud-phase tail of the claim is very hard to isolate.

title: Bloom slicks cut evaporation below bulk heat-flux formulas
untested: Latent heat flux has not been measured directly (eddy covariance or gradient) inside versus outside natural slicks; the 5-15 percent overestimate, its wind-speed range and its scaling with surfactant concentration and slick cover remain unquantified.

papers.title: Skin-layer observations: Trichodesmium blooms gave a skin about 0.95 C warmer and fresher and inhibited evaporation (inferred from salinity); no direct latent heat flux or surfactant dose-response

Sea Surface Scanner catamaran data: natural surfactants above 200 ug Teq per litre cut CO2 transfer velocity by 23 percent, slicks by a further 62 percent; tested gas exchange, not evaporation or heat

web.text: Surface films are known to retard evaporation in reservoirs and lab tanks, and ocean observations show warmer, fresher skin layers and reduced gas exchange under blooms and slicks. A quantified evaporative heat-flux deficit at sea, scaled to surfactant concentration, appears not to have been published, and wind-driven mixing above about 5 m/s likely destroys much of the film effect.

why: Strength: the 200 ug Teq threshold and gas-exchange precedent give a concrete, measurable design; risk: the effect on evaporation may be smaller than 5 percent or vanish at moderate wind, and flux measurements inside slicks are hard.

title: Atmospheric river landfalls drive coastal chlorophyll, more with northerly wind
untested: The orientation contrast has been shown for central-southern Chile in a few events, but no multi-decade regression across Chile, California and Iberia tests whether AR count and orientation explain at least 20 percent of interannual variance in 4-week nearshore chlorophyll.

papers.title: Central-southern Chile (33-40 S): tilted (northerly-wind) ARs gave coastally trapped plumes and raised surface nitrate, silicic acid and chlorophyll-a more than zonal ARs; a few events and in situ sampling, no interannual variance explained, no other regions

Storm Desmond atmospheric river at an Irish coastal observatory: record discharge, doubled stratification and plume export; physical and water-quality cascade for one event, no multi-year chlorophyll statistics
Storm rainfall triggers seasonal stratification on the NW European shelf in 88 percent of years; supports rain-driven buoyancy effects but not chlorophyll or ARs specifically

web.text: A 2025 Chile study already reports that northerly-wind (tilted) ARs raise nitrate, silicic acid and chlorophyll more than zonal ARs, and an Irish case study shows large AR-driven plume and stratification changes. A web search found no multi-year regression of nearshore chlorophyll on AR count for California or Iberia, and winter cloud cover limits ocean-colour data.

why: Strength: AR catalogues and ocean colour archives make the regression easy and a Chile precedent supports the direction; risk: the 20 percent variance threshold may fail because winter cloud limits chlorophyll data and plumes add turbidity that confounds retrieval.

title: Microbial heat speeds thaw of carbon-rich permafrost soils
untested: The core idea has been tested in Greenland organic soils and middens, but not with the proposed live-versus-sterilised twin cores in insulated incubators, nor with field matching of organic and mineral plots for air temperature and snow to isolate a 5-20 percent deeper thaw.

papers.title: Hollesen et al.: heat production measured in contrasting organic permafrost soils in Greenland; microbial heat can amplify thaw and decomposition (abstract via Copenhagen repository summary; full text paywalled and not read)
Greenland organic archaeological deposits: O2, CO2 and heat production tracked together; microbial heat production correlated with carbon content; no sterile controls or thaw-depth field comparison
ORCHIDEE-MICT land model: microbial heat lowers soil carbon, warms deeper layers, and brings earlier permafrost loss; modelling only, no measurements

web.text: Hollesen and colleagues measured microbial heat in Greenland organic soils and concluded it can amplify thaw, and a recent land-surface model finds microbial heat warms deep soil and advances permafrost loss. Heat from respiration is small relative to atmospheric forcing and is lost by conduction in the field, so the size of any effect on active-layer depth in peat versus mineral plots at equal air temperature is still uncertain.

links.label: Heat from SOC decomposition model study
Arctic organic deposits and microbial heat

why: Strength: calorimetry on live versus sterile cores is a clean falsifiable test with prior supporting data; risk: the effect is already reported, and field heat dissipation plus insulating peat confound any thaw-depth difference.

title: Virus-killed blooms raise sea spray organics and shift cloud droplets
untested: Field data have not compared virus-terminated with nutrient- or grazer-terminated blooms at matched chlorophyll for aerosol organic fraction or cloud droplet number; the 20 percent and 10 percent magnitudes and the sign of the droplet change are untested.

papers.title: Virus-infected cultures of diatom, coccolithophore and chlorophyte hosts gave aerosolised organics with larger activation diameter, higher molar mass and lower hygroscopicity in 3 of 5 pairs; lab nebulised DOM only, no bubble bursting, no clouds
Organic mass fraction of submicron sea spray correlates with senescent-cell index (chlorophyllide) in the subarctic Pacific; did not separate viral from other causes of senescence
Organic enrichment of sea spray rises with bloom demise; suggests viral infection as a driver but did not measure viruses
Cloud droplet number at Mace Head about doubles in the productive season, showing marine biology affects cloud microphysics; no viral or bloom-phase attribution

web.text: Lab work shows virus-infected phytoplankton change the properties of aerosolised organic matter and reduce hygroscopicity, and field correlations tie sea-spray organic fraction to bloom senescence. Whether viral termination specifically changes cloud droplet number against grazer- or nutrient-terminated blooms is not tested, and lower hygroscopicity could push droplet number either way.

links.label: Marine biology and cloud droplets at Mace Head

why: Strength: organic enrichment after infection has lab and field support; risk: matching bloom termination modes in the field is hard and the droplet-number sign and size are uncertain.

title: Dark cyanobacterial crust boosts midday dryland sensible heat flux
untested: Sensible heat flux itself has not been compared between intact dark cyanobacterial crust and disturbed or light crust; the 20-40 W/m2 difference and the cooling after crust loss are unmeasured, and moisture, roughness and ground-heat storage could cancel the albedo effect.

papers.title: Two-year moss-biocrust study: biocrust albedo 43 percent lower than bare soil, raising net radiation and altering energy balance; moss not cyanobacteria, and results reported as radiation terms rather than a clean dry-season sensible heat contrast

Two-decade warming experiment on the Colorado Plateau: shift to lightly pigmented early-successional cyanobacteria raised surface brightness and surface temperature about 0.3 C per 10 percent cover, via lower moisture; remote sensing, no flux measurements, and the sign of brightness effect is opposite to the dark-crust case

web.text: Biocrusts, especially dark moss and cyanobacterial ones, lower albedo and increase net radiation, and warming experiments show crust community shifts alter surface temperature. Direct sensible heat flux comparisons between intact dark crust and disturbed crust were not found, and most of the extra absorbed energy may go into soil heat storage and longwave loss or into latent heat after rain.

links.label: Biocrust degradation and surface temperature feedback

why: Strength: albedo contrast and flux instruments make a direct paired test easy; risk: patch-scale H differences are small versus measurement error and the partition of extra net radiation among H, soil heat and moisture is uncertain.

title: Thaw-slump sulfuric acid weathering offsets permafrost CO2 drawdown
untested: Regional trends and headwater acidification are documented, but the paired slump-versus-intact design with SO4:HCO3 ratios, d34S and d13C-DIC to partition sulfuric versus carbonic acid, and the 2-5x ratio and 10-30 percent CO2 offset, have not been reported for matched catchments.

papers.title: Mackenzie basin 60-year sulfate record: sulfate flux up 45 percent with 2.3 C warming, largest in catchments with thermokarst and rapid exposure; basin-scale, no paired slump streams or isotope partitioning

Yukon and Mackenzie headwaters: abrupt sulfide oxidation, pH about 3 seeps, and acid-driven carbonate dissolution speeding CO2 emissions; abstract only (paywalled), a different mechanism scale from slump streams
Qinghai-Tibet rivers: weathering CO2 drawdown about 35 percent of river CO2 emission and rising with thaw; used carbonic-acid framing and isotope modelling on a plateau, not slump versus intact pairs
Mackenzie DIC radiocarbon and d13C: old carbon from organic oxidation with some carbonate weathering input; did not partition sulfuric versus carbonic acid

web.text: Sulfide oxidation and sulfuric-acid carbonate dissolution are documented in thawing Canadian permafrost catchments, with sulfate rising strongly where thermokarst exposes rock. A direct, matched slump versus intact quantification of the carbonic versus sulfuric share and the net CO2 offset is not evident in the literature found.

links.label: Rock weathering and river CO2, Nature 2026

why: Strength: the chemistry is well grounded and the isotope design is standard; risk: much of the headline finding is already published at regional scale, and the exact 2-5x and 10-30 percent figures depend heavily on lithology.

title: Proglacial dust feeds Greenland ice algae and darker ice
untested: The mechanism links (local proglacial dust, mineral P, algal biomass) are supported, but no study regresses year-to-year algal bloom or albedo on proglacial plain area and spring wind with melt days controlled; the 20-50 percent and 0.02-0.05 magnitudes and the feedback loop are untested.

papers.title: Local proglacial dust (REE and airmass evidence) delivered about 1.2 mg P per m2 per year to the southwest ice sheet, enough to fuel observed algal cell densities; two years of data, no interannual regression with bloom or albedo
Mineral phosphorus in surface ice correlates with glacier algal biomass across the southwest ablation zone; spatial link, not year-to-year or tied to proglacial source area
NW Greenland nano-molar nutrient data suggest dissolved N and P released by ablation exceed algal uptake, so macronutrients may not limit algae; counter-evidence to the dust-P limitation step
Dark Zone albedo budget: cryoconite and ice densification dominate darkening, then algae; mineral dust particles do not directly darken; indicates dust acts, if at all, via algae

web.text: Local dust from proglacial plains delivers phosphorus and mineral P correlates with algal biomass, but a 2026 study argues that dissolved nutrients released by ablation are unlikely to limit algae, and a Dark Zone albedo budget gives algae a smaller role than cryoconite and ice densification. A Greenland-wide model shows bloom magnitude following ablation-zone area and melt, which is the main confounder for any dust signal.

links.label: Local dust delivers P to the ice sheet
Mineral phosphorus drives glacier algal blooms
Ablation supplies N and P to ice algae

why: Strength: remote-sensing and wind data make an interannual regression feasible and each causal link has partial support; risk: bloom size is dominated by melt and ablation area, and recent work argues P is not limiting.

title: Peak meltwater flow lets more Greenland methane escape unoxidised
untested: No study has measured the oxidised versus degassed fraction of subglacial methane along a Greenland outlet river at low versus peak discharge; the over-half versus under-20 percent split and the claim that emissions outgrow the methanotroph sink with ice loss are untested.

papers.title: Methane oxidation in land-terminating glacial runoff (lake and river): river oxidation may cut emissions by up to 53 percent; measured net activity at sites but not as a function of discharge or residence time

Greenland subglacial catchment: methane-supersaturated water exported continuously through the melt season with pulses at flushing events; quantified export at the portal, not downstream oxidation versus degassing (abstract only, paywalled)

web.text: Subglacial methane exits Greenland in meltwater, discharge pulses flush it out, and downstream oxidation can remove a large share in some rivers. How the oxidised fraction changes with discharge and transit time has not been quantified, and fast turbulent degassing near the portal could dominate at all flows, which would make the discharge dependence weaker than predicted.

why: Strength: a clear station-by-station design with isotope fractionation can falsify it; risk: the over-half degassing figure depends on a residence-time model and river reaeration, and the 2024 river data suggest oxidation can be substantial.

title: Ponded thaw slumps raise methylmercury via sulfate and iron reducers
untested: Higher methylmercury in thawed ponded ground is already documented; what remains untested is the specific sulfate-reducer and Fe-reducer dependence (molybdate and sulfate amendments), the 5-20 year chronosequence on slumps, and the 3-10x ratio on one mercury-rich landscape.

papers.title: Twelve NW Canada peatlands: soil %MeHg was 0.1 percent on permafrost plateaus, 0.7 percent in thawed bogs, 2.0 percent in fens; methylators included methanogens, not mainly sulfate reducers; no sulfate manipulation (abstract read)

Nunavik lithalsa chronosequence of 175 soils across thermokarst development and pond revegetation, with THg, MeHg and S; asked how feature evolution shapes net MeHg production, no hgcAB or inhibitor test
Two Canadian sub-Arctic thermokarst lakes: hgcAB and merAB metagenomes and qPCR followed seasonal MMHg changes; lakes not slumps, no sulfate or molybdate manipulation

Tibetan thermokarst lakes: elevated MeHg with anaerobic incubations plus inhibitors; sulfate reducers dominated in one lake but syntrophs and methanogens contributed about 57 percent in another, so sulfate-reducer dependence varies

web.text: Thaw ponds, thermokarst lakes and thawed peatlands show higher methylmercury fractions than frozen ground, and hgcA-carrying communities respond to thaw. Inhibitor work shows methylators differ by site, with methanogens and syntrophs important alongside sulfate reducers, so a strict sulfate dependence is uncertain.

why: Strength: methodology is standard and the headline elevation is well supported; risk: the elevation is already shown and the claim that sulfate and iron reducers are the main drivers conflicts with evidence for methanogen and syntroph methylators.

title: Thaw-slump acid weathering weakens permafrost CO2 sink
untested: Regional trends and headwater acidification are documented, but the paired slump-versus-intact design with SO4:HCO3 ratios, d34S and d13C-DIC to partition sulfuric versus carbonic acid, and the 2-5x ratio and 10-30 percent CO2 offset, have not been reported for matched catchments.

papers.title: Mackenzie basin 60-year sulfate record: sulfate flux up 45 percent with 2.3 C warming, largest in catchments with thermokarst and rapid exposure; basin-scale, no paired slump streams or isotope partitioning

Yukon and Mackenzie headwaters: abrupt sulfide oxidation, pH about 3 seeps, and acid-driven carbonate dissolution speeding CO2 emissions; abstract only (paywalled), a different mechanism scale from slump streams
Qinghai-Tibet rivers: weathering CO2 drawdown about 35 percent of river CO2 emission and rising with thaw; used carbonic-acid framing and isotope modelling on a plateau, not slump versus intact pairs
Mackenzie DIC radiocarbon and d13C: old carbon from organic oxidation with some carbonate weathering input; did not partition sulfuric versus carbonic acid

web.text: Sulfide oxidation and sulfuric-acid carbonate dissolution are documented in thawing Canadian permafrost catchments, with sulfate rising strongly where thermokarst exposes rock. A direct, matched slump versus intact quantification of the carbonic versus sulfuric share and the net CO2 offset is not evident in the literature found.

links.label: Rock weathering and river CO2, Nature 2026

why: Strength: the chemistry is well grounded and the isotope design is standard; risk: much of the headline finding is already published at regional scale, and the exact 2-5x and 10-30 percent figures depend heavily on lithology.

title: Proglacial dust phosphorus fuels Greenland ice algae darkening
untested: The mechanism links (local proglacial dust, mineral P, algal biomass) are supported, but no study regresses year-to-year algal bloom or albedo on proglacial plain area and spring wind with melt days controlled; the 20-50 percent and 0.02-0.05 magnitudes and the feedback loop are untested.

papers.title: Local proglacial dust (REE and airmass evidence) delivered about 1.2 mg P per m2 per year to the southwest ice sheet, enough to fuel observed algal cell densities; two years of data, no interannual regression with bloom or albedo
Mineral phosphorus in surface ice correlates with glacier algal biomass across the southwest ablation zone; spatial link, not year-to-year or tied to proglacial source area
NW Greenland nano-molar nutrient data suggest dissolved N and P released by ablation exceed algal uptake, so macronutrients may not limit algae; counter-evidence to the dust-P limitation step
Dark Zone albedo budget: cryoconite and ice densification dominate darkening, then algae; mineral dust particles do not directly darken; indicates dust acts, if at all, via algae

web.text: Local dust from proglacial plains delivers phosphorus and mineral P correlates with algal biomass, but a 2026 study argues that dissolved nutrients released by ablation are unlikely to limit algae, and a Dark Zone albedo budget gives algae a smaller role than cryoconite and ice densification. A Greenland-wide model shows bloom magnitude following ablation-zone area and melt, which is the main confounder for any dust signal.

links.label: Local dust delivers P to the ice sheet
Mineral phosphorus drives glacier algal blooms
Ablation supplies N and P to ice algae

why: Strength: remote-sensing and wind data make an interannual regression feasible and each causal link has partial support; risk: bloom size is dominated by melt and ablation area, and recent work argues P is not limiting.

title: Fast meltwater flow limits methane oxidation at Greenland outlets
untested: No study has measured the oxidised versus degassed fraction of subglacial methane along a Greenland outlet river at low versus peak discharge; the over-half versus under-20 percent split and the claim that emissions outgrow the methanotroph sink with ice loss are untested.

papers.title: Methane oxidation in land-terminating glacial runoff (lake and river): river oxidation may cut emissions by up to 53 percent; measured net activity at sites but not as a function of discharge or residence time

Greenland subglacial catchment: methane-supersaturated water exported continuously through the melt season with pulses at flushing events; quantified export at the portal, not downstream oxidation versus degassing (abstract only, paywalled)

web.text: Subglacial methane exits Greenland in meltwater, discharge pulses flush it out, and downstream oxidation can remove a large share in some rivers. How the oxidised fraction changes with discharge and transit time has not been quantified, and fast turbulent degassing near the portal could dominate at all flows, which would make the discharge dependence weaker than predicted.

why: Strength: a clear station-by-station design with isotope fractionation can falsify it; risk: the over-half degassing figure depends on a residence-time model and river reaeration, and the 2024 river data suggest oxidation can be substantial.

title: Thermokarst ponding boosts methylmercury via sulfate reduction
untested: Higher methylmercury in thawed ponded ground is already documented; what remains untested is the specific sulfate-reducer and Fe-reducer dependence (molybdate and sulfate amendments), the 5-20 year chronosequence on slumps, and the 3-10x ratio on one mercury-rich landscape.

title: Farm ammonia lofted by monsoon adds upper-troposphere cloud seeds
untested: Models and chamber work already give this mechanism, but a matched observational comparison of measured CCN at 0.2 percent supersaturation in monsoon outflow versus low-NH3 convective outflow, binned by NH3 and SO2, is missing, as is a cloud radiative effect attributed to NH3 beyond sulfate.

papers.title: EMAC global model: convective NH3 raised upper-tropospheric particle formation by 1-3 orders of magnitude, doubling aerosol number and giving a 2.5-fold CCN increase over high-emission regions; model only, no observed CCN comparison
CLOUD chamber: HNO3-H2SO4-NH3 nucleate particles synergistically, grow to CCN size with trace sulfate, and act as efficient ice nuclei; laboratory plus simulations, no matched aircraft CCN test

In-situ monsoon outflow observations with trajectories and modelling show pollution-enhanced new particle formation and growth to cloud-relevant sizes; did not contrast NH3-rich versus NH3-poor outflow CCN at fixed SO2
Asian Tropopause Aerosol Layer simulation: NH3-driven particle formation raised CCN by up to 80 percent; modelling only

web.text: CLOUD chamber and chemistry-climate model studies show that convectively lofted ammonia drives upper-tropospheric particle formation and can raise CCN by tens of percent to several-fold over monsoon regions, and in-situ outflow data support pollution-enhanced particle formation. A direct observed CCN contrast and a quantified cloud-brightening forcing term are still lacking, and upper-tropospheric CCN counts at fixed supersaturation are sparse.

links.label: Global NH3 impact on upper-troposphere aerosol

why: Strength: chamber, model and in-situ results already point the same way; risk: the observed-CCN contrast and any net forcing from NH3 are hard to isolate from sulfate and nitrate and upper-troposphere CCN data are scarce.

title: Falling acid-rain sulfate changed lake phosphorus release by sediment Fe:S
untested: No paired-core or dated-core study of softwater lakes has tested whether post-1990 sulfate decline raised anoxic P release where porewater Fe:S is above 1 and lowered it where below 1; the 20 percent threshold and Fe:S breakpoint of 1 are untested.

papers.title: Mackinawite (FeS) binds phosphate with capacity comparable to moderately crystalline Fe oxides, reduced about 75 percent by sorbed organic carbon; lab sorption only, not tied to sulfate decline or lake release rates

Sulfate-amended mesocosms of eutrophic lake sediment: higher sulfate gave more P release via sulfide-mediated FeP loss; tested sulfate increase in eutrophic lakes, not decline in softwater lakes or an Fe:S split (abstract only, paywalled)

web.text: Sulfate-driven P mobilisation and FeS sequestration of phosphate are both documented, so the Fe:S-dependent sign is chemically reasonable. Evidence concerns rising sulfate or lab minerals, and the prediction that declining acid-rain sulfate increased P release in iron-rich softwater lakes seems untested; long records are patchy and stratification, DOC and eutrophication trends confound them.

links.label: Sulfate-induced P mobilisation in eutrophic lakes

why: Strength: a well-defined Fe:S switch gives a sharp falsifiable split and no direct test exists; risk: few lakes have both long deposition and hypolimnetic P records, and warming, DOC and stratification changes swamp a 20 percent signal.

title: Falling SO2 lowers aerosol iron solubility over iron-limited oceans
untested: No study compares marine aerosol fractional Fe solubility before and after the SO2 declines (Europe, North America, China, 2020 shipping rules) at matched dust loading; the 10-30 percent decline and its attribution to sulfate rather than nitrate or aerosol pH are untested.

papers.title: Aerosol Fe dissolution in East Asia: nitrate now contributes about 1.5 times more than sulfate in urban aerosol and about 68 percent of the modelled solubility enhancement in dust relative to preindustrial; challenges the sulfur-driven paradigm and offers a competing mechanism that would offset SO2 cuts; urban data, not marine trend data
GEOTRACES North Atlantic aerosol Fe isotopes show a small soluble anthropogenic combustion Fe component likely underestimated in deposition models; one-time section, no before-after solubility trend

web.text: Acid processing by sulfate and nitrate raises Fe solubility, and combustion Fe is a significant soluble fraction in the North Atlantic. Recent work shows nitrate is replacing sulfate as the main acid agent in East Asia, so falling SO2 may not lower solubility, and no repeated-cruise or station trend in marine aerosol solubility around 2005 or 2020 was found.

links.label: Anthropogenic aerosol Fe in North Atlantic

why: Strength: archived GEOTRACES and island-station samples could test a before-after change; risk: solubility depends on dust, source mix, nitrate and aerosol water, so a clean sulfate-attributed 10-30 percent decline is unlikely to show.

title: Basalt spreading darkens bare cropland soil and offsets carbon removal
untested: No study has measured albedo change after crushed rock is spread on cropland, or converted it to CO2-equivalent against the weathering carbon removal. Biochar darkening is the only analogue, and basalt is much less dark and mixes in differently.

papers.title: Albedo impact of biochar (30 t/ha cut mean annual albedo by 0.05 and trimmed climate benefit 13-22%); did not test any rock powder.
Four-year US Corn Belt basalt trial (50 t/ha/yr) measuring cation loss, yield and CDR; did not measure albedo or radiative forcing.
Process model of enhanced rock weathering with ecohydrology and soil moisture; no surface-albedo term.

web.text: Biochar work shows that dark amendments at 30 t/ha cut soil albedo enough to erode a measurable share of climate benefit. Enhanced weathering trials and models report cation loss, yield and CDR but no albedo effect. Searches of Europe PMC for enhanced weathering together with soil or surface albedo give only a handful of unrelated hits.

why: Strength: a cheap paired-albedometer trial would settle it and the biochar analogy is quantified; risk: basalt is mid-grey (albedo about 0.1-0.2) so the darkening on already-dark soils may be negligible and the effect decays fast, making the offset small.

title: Basalt dust on snow melts fields out earlier
untested: No trial has put crushed basalt on snowpack at agricultural rates, or measured melt-out timing, frozen-soil runoff losses and basalt recovery in runoff. Whether enhanced weathering operators spread on snow at all is unverified.

papers.title: Colorado River runoff under dust radiative forcing in snow: peak runoff about 3 weeks earlier with heavier dust; modelled, not a basalt or farm trial.
Four-year basalt field trial in the US Corn Belt (fall application); no snow, albedo or melt measurements.

web.text: Dust on snow lowers albedo and advances melt by weeks in mountain snowpacks, so the physics is established at much lower loads. No enhanced weathering paper addresses spreading on snow-covered or frozen ground; the combined Europe PMC query returns few hits and none on this.

why: Strength: dust-on-snow physics is solid and a plot trial is straightforward; risk: the premise that crushed rock is routinely spread on snow is unverified, and 5 kg/m2 may be buried or washed in rather than concentrated.

title: Air pollution haze slows UV breakdown of dryland litter
untested: Nobody has tested whether aerosol attenuation of UV and sunlight changes litter photodegradation, with filters mimicking haze spectra or along natural haze gradients. Haze also adds diffuse light and dust that could offset the UV loss.

papers.title: UNEP assessment chapter on UV, climate and terrestrial ecosystems, covering UV-driven litter breakdown; treats aerosol only generally and tests no haze-litter link.
12-month litterbag test of UV-B on wheat and maize straw (UV-B raised mass loss 14-19% without soil contact); did not vary aerosols or haze.

web.text: Many exclusion experiments show sunlight and UV raise litter mass loss, so a smaller dose should slow it. Reviews of UV effects note that clouds and ozone modulate exposure but I found no study linking aerosol load to litter photodegradation.

why: Strength: filter-based litterbag design is feasible and directionally grounded in UV-exclusion work; risk: the haze-driven dose reduction is modest relative to cloud and season, and microbial decay will dominate in many sites.

title: Cracks in dry Vertisols boost atmospheric methane uptake
untested: No study has measured CH4 flux over open versus closed shrinkage cracks in a Vertisol, or crack-wall methanotroph activity. The claim of a 2-5x uptake boost is untested.

papers.title: Conference abstract: nighttime thermal convection in soil fractures enhances gas flux, suggested for CO2 in clayey soils; did not measure methane.
Review of soil-aquifer processes under Vertisols: cracks as preferential flow and evaporation paths; methane not addressed.

web.text: Cracks are known to speed gas transport and to ventilate soil by thermal convection, but only CO2 and oxygen studies exist. I found no methane uptake measurement tied to crack state in Vertisols; the topic overlap in Europe PMC is about 2 papers.

why: Strength: chamber-over-crack design is clean and the gap is real; risk: dry-season Vertisol matrix already dries and takes up methane, and crack gas can also carry methane out or shift moisture, confounding a crack effect.

title: Volcanic acid fallout starves nitrogen fixers of molybdenum
untested: Mo availability and free-living nitrogen fixation have not been measured along a volcanic acid-deposition transect. The Masaya work covers pH, bases, sulfate, chloride and fluoride but not Mo.

papers.title: Mo and P co-limit free-living N fixation in Panamanian forests; shows Mo availability controls fixation but involves no volcanic acid or pH gradient.
Masaya Andosols exposed to volcanic acid: pH and base cations fall, sulfate and fluoride retained, HCl main acidifier; no Mo or N fixation data.

web.text: Mo limits free-living fixation and molybdate sorption rises as pH falls, both well known. But the Masaya soils are mainly acidified by HCl, and retained sulfate competes with molybdate for sorption sites, which could raise rather than lower available Mo. No test of the link was found.

why: Strength: the Masaya transect and Mo-addition factorial are a sharp test; risk: sulfate competition, HCl rather than SO2 acidification, and volcanic Mo input could reverse the sign.

title: Clay-fixed ammonium weakens fertiliser inhibition of methane uptake
untested: No study has compared ammonium inhibition of atmospheric-level methane oxidation across vermiculitic, illitic and kaolinitic soils, or tested K-blocked versus Ca-vermiculite. Ammonium fixation has not been linked to methanotroph inhibition.

papers.title: Ammonium and non-ammonium salts cut forest-soil methane uptake largely through ion exchange displacing ammonium; clay mineralogy and ammonium fixation not tested.
Review of nitrogen as a regulator of methane oxidation (inhibition, but also N limitation); no treatment of clay-fixed ammonium.

web.text: Ammonium inhibition of upland methane uptake is well documented and exchange-site behaviour already shapes it. Ammonium fixation by 2:1 clays is a separate, well-known soil process. The two literatures barely meet: a combined Europe PMC search finds only a few papers, none testing clay type.

why: Strength: a controlled sand-plus-clay microcosm cleanly isolates the clay effect; risk: nitrite from methanotroph ammonia oxidation, not ammonium itself, may drive inhibition, and fixed ammonium can be re-released.

title: Large soil aggregates have anoxic cores that release iron-bound phosphate
untested: Nobody has mapped Fe(II) and labile P against aggregate size and anoxic volume in one aerobic upland soil, with crushing as a control. Aggregate-size P studies exist but do not link release to anoxic cores.

papers.title: Phosphorus fractions across aggregate sizes under rice, maize and soybean: Fe/Al-bound P concentrated in large aggregates and shifted under aerobic-anaerobic cycling; no oxygen mapping or Fe(II) test.
Review of anoxic microsites and their role in Fe, N and C cycles; conceptual, no aggregate-size P experiment.

web.text: Anoxic microsites and Fe-driven P mobilisation under reducing conditions are both established, and large aggregates retain Fe-bound P. The specific claim that aggregate interiors under moist but drained conditions release P in proportion to anoxic volume is not directly shown. Overlap in Europe PMC is about 2 papers.

why: Strength: optode and DGT imaging with a crushed control is a sharp test; risk: at 65% water-filled pores most aggregates may stay oxic, and released P may re-sorb or be masked by organic P.

title: Nitrate-fed roots precipitate calcite in the rhizosphere of calcareous soils
untested: Nobody has compared rhizosphere carbonate content and delta-13C between nitrate- and ammonium-fed roots in calcareous soil. Root respiration CO2 may push the opposite way and dissolve calcite.

papers.title: Nitrate raised rhizosphere pH by 0.19-0.78 units and ammonium lowered it by 0.16-0.38 in wheat and lupin; priming effect studied, carbonate not.
Incubations show organic residue decomposition acidifies soil and dissolves calcite via respired CO2; no plants or N form comparison.

web.text: Nitrate alkalinisation and ammonium acidification at roots are well documented. Whether this crosses calcite saturation, given high rhizosphere CO2 and bicarbonate buffering, is unshown; recent work stresses respiration-driven carbonate dissolution. I found no rhizolith or rhizosheath study tied to N form.

why: Strength: rhizobox design with 13C carbonate is feasible; risk: respired CO2 and bicarbonate buffering likely outweigh the pH rise, so net precipitation may not occur.

title: Snow reflects UV onto standing litter and speeds its breakdown
untested: No experiment has used real snow with UV-transparent versus UV-blocking films on standing litter. The only albedo test used artificial surfaces and found a small effect.

papers.title: Sorghum litter over aluminium, white and black surfaces mimicking snow: 1.4-2.5% more mass loss over the UV-reflective surface; snow itself never tested.
Five-month desert litter study with warming and added winter snow cover; looked at decomposition rate, not UV reflection.
UNEP assessment chapter covering UV-driven litter breakdown; snow reflection only speculative.

web.text: Photodegradation of standing litter is well documented and snow reflectance has been proposed as an amplifier. The one albedo test showed only a few percent extra mass loss, much smaller than the 8-20% predicted. No snow trial exists.

why: Strength: black-cloth control isolates snow reflection well; risk: winter UV is low and litter is cold and dry, so the real effect is likely much smaller than predicted.

title: Snowmelt-dominated soils carry carbonate deeper than rain-fed soils
untested: No pedon-database regression has isolated snow fraction on depth to the carbonate horizon at fixed precipitation and temperature. Cold-water calcite solubility versus infiltration depth has not been separated in columns.

papers.title: Seasonal bias in pedogenic carbonate formation in central New Mexico soils (I could read only the title and record); concerns timing, not snow versus rain depth.
Process model of soil inorganic carbon under climate change with daily water balance; no snow fraction test of carbonate depth.

web.text: Carbonate depth is known to relate to precipitation and seasonality, but depth-rainfall relations are weak and contested in the literature. Snowmelt infiltrating at low evapotranspiration should wet deeper. I found no direct test of the snow fraction effect; overlap in Europe PMC is about 4 papers.

links.label: Breecker et al. seasonal carbonate record

why: Strength: the infiltration argument is physically sound and testable with public data; risk: carbonate depth also reflects dust input, parent material and paleoclimate inheritance, which can swamp a 10-30 cm effect.

title: Clear nights deposit more dew on litter and speed night decay
untested: No study has binned nights by longwave loss or used a longwave-opaque shelter to show cloud cover gates litter wetness and night-time CO2 efflux. Dew studies on litter exist but without this cloud link.

papers.title: Namib litter: fungi respond within minutes to fog and dew moisture and decompose surface litter; cloud or longwave control not examined.
Standing grass litter fungi and decomposition under non-rainfall versus rain moisture regimes in the Namib; no radiative driver.
Global eddy covariance evidence for soil water vapour adsorption at high humidity; not litter, no cloud test.

web.text: Non-rainfall moisture is known to activate litter decay in drylands, and radiative cooling under clear skies is the textbook dew mechanism. The link between nocturnal cloud, litter moisture and respiration has not been measured; counts show only about 2 overlapping papers.

why: Strength: well-grounded physics and a feasible instrumented test with a shelter treatment; risk: litter hygroscopic water uptake can occur without dew, so clear-versus-cloudy differences may be small at RH below 80%.

title: Atmospheric rivers raise winter ocean CO2 uptake despite warming
untested: Nobody has composited air-sea CO2 flux at Station Papa on atmospheric-river days or measured the net of faster gas exchange against surface warming. Only storm studies from tropical cyclones and AR-marine heatwave studies exist.

papers.title: Tropical cyclone wind-pump effect on pCO2 and air-sea CO2 flux at two moorings; tropical storms, not atmospheric rivers or Papa.
Atmospheric rivers cool through cloud and warm through reduced heat loss, shaping marine heatwaves; no carbon flux analysed.
Storm-resolving model: tropical cyclones boost CO2 flux 20-40 times and cool the surface; not atmospheric rivers.

web.text: Storm studies show wind-driven gas exchange dominates, and AR work confirms opposing cloud and heat-flux effects on SST. No paper combines them for CO2; strict searches for atmospheric rivers with air-sea CO2 flux return near zero relevant hits.

why: Strength: existing mooring data and an AR catalogue allow a quick test; risk: AR rainfall freshening and mixed-layer deepening could shift pCO2 more than the predicted warming, and AR days are few.

title: Dam-cut river sediment slows carbon sinking on river-fed margins
untested: No experiment or trap comparison has tied river sediment decline after damming to lithogenic ballast and carbon transfer on the adjacent slope. Most river sediment settles on the shelf, so the signal at 500-1000 m may be tiny.

papers.title: Mineral ballast in surface export from thorium data: ballast matters most in the North Atlantic, unballasted export often dominates; no rivers or dams.
Clay added to seawater raised TEP tenfold and formed sinking organoclay flocs; microcosm, no river loads or respiration per metre.
Review of large-river delta fronts, Changjiang and Mississippi, as recorders of human change; discusses carbon fluxes, not ballast or dams.

web.text: Ballast effects on sinking are well known but vary strongly by region, and sediment-load decline after damming is well documented. The two have not been joined in an experiment or trap comparison.

why: Strength: the roller-tank experiment is a clear lab test; risk: field attribution to dams is confounded by shelf trapping, resuspension and productivity changes, and lithogenic ballast can also stimulate flocculation, so the sign at depth is uncertain.

title: Ocean acidification cuts sea-to-air methylamine emissions
untested: Nobody has measured how seawater pH changes amine emission to air, or the dissolved-to-gas ratio across pH 7.7-8.1. Biological changes in amine supply could offset the chemistry.

papers.title: Review of ocean acidification effects on DMS, N2O, ammonia and halocarbons; amines not quantified.
Flux-system study of ammonia and amines from model aqueous solutions with CIMS; shows Henry's-law uncertainty, no pH series or seawater.

web.text: Amine protonation at seawater pH follows acid-base equilibrium, and the volatile fraction does fall as pH drops. Reviews cover OA effects on ammonia and DMS, but I found no pH-controlled seawater amine flux measurement. Henry's-law constants for amines are uncertain by orders of magnitude.

links.label: OA and marine trace gases review

why: Strength: simple acid-base prediction with a clean lab test; risk: total dissolved amine production by plankton, surface-film effects and warming may dominate real-ocean changes, and uncertain constants weaken the numbers.

title: Fine volcanic ash suppresses soil methane uptake
untested: No study has measured methane uptake under graded ash thickness and grain size on upland soil. Sulfate and fluoride toxicity versus diffusion blockage is unseparated.

papers.title: PhD thesis on volcanic sulfate and fluoride on soil gas fluxes: tephra-like sulfate and fluoride doses did not change peat CH4 flux; a wet ash layer slowed CO2 release; not upland methane uptake.
Review of methane cycling in temperate forests; soils are sinks with varying controls, no volcanic ash effect.

web.text: Upland methane uptake is controlled by gas diffusion, and wet fine layers and compaction cut it. Ash effects have been studied for CO2 and peat chemistry but not for atmospheric methane uptake.

links.label: Myers thesis, volcanic S and F on soil gas

why: Strength: diffusion mechanism is well grounded and core-cap lab tests are easy; risk: net methane emission under ash is a strong claim, and the field test depends on a rare eruption.

title: Fresh labile carbon primes rock organic carbon oxidation
untested: No incubation has partitioned CO2 from shale with and without labile carbon by 14C and 13C, nor tested priming of kerogen in sterile controls. Rock carbon oxidation studies have not added labile carbon.

papers.title: Model of shale regolith carbon: petrogenic and pyrite oxidation CO2 smaller than soil respiration fluxes; no priming experiment.
Rhenium tracing shows glaciated catchments oxidise rock-bound organic carbon 2-3 times faster; no labile carbon test.
Goldschmidt 2023 abstract on two-stage oxidation of petrogenic carbon (priming suggested; I could only read the title).

web.text: Petrogenic carbon oxidation is microbially mediated and priming is common for young soil carbon. Work on kerogen mostly addresses temperature, erosion and water. I found no experiment adding labile carbon to shale.

why: Strength: three-source partitioning gives a decisive test; risk: aromatic kerogen is highly recalcitrant, so labile carbon may simply favour microbial growth on glucose with little extra rock-carbon CO2.

title: Sulfate from glacial pyrite oxidation suppresses lake methane emission
untested: No survey of proglacial lakes has compared methane emission by bedrock sulfide content, or run molybdate slurry tests. Lithology is confounded with organic carbon, depth and glacier cover.

papers.title: Synthesis of proglacial lake methane fluxes in Alaska and Greenland; sulfate and lithology not examined.
Tibetan proglacial lake sediments: methane oxidation and sulfide-oxidising methanotroph genomes; no emission or lithology comparison.
Peat mesocosm dosed with volcanic sulfate: no significant change in CH4 flux, against earlier reports of suppression.

web.text: Sulfate reducers outcompeting methanogens is textbook, and glacial sulfide oxidation makes sulfate-rich water. Proglacial lake methane work exists, but none compares lithology or sulfate. A peat dosing test found no sulfate effect, so the suppression is not guaranteed.

why: Strength: sulfate competition is well founded and the molybdate test is decisive; risk: proglacial lakes emit little methane to begin with and matched lakes by lithology are hard to find, so the field comparison is noisy.

title: Forest canopy cuts thermal-stress cracking of surface rock
untested: No paired shaded versus exposed boulder study has counted acoustic-emission cracking events or tested canopy removal. Temperature damping is documented, but cracking is not.

papers.title: Instrumented single granite boulder in full sun: nearly 12,000 acoustic emissions in four months, mostly as the rock cooled in the afternoon; no shaded control.
Ivy cover on limestone walls cut freezing events 26% and lab stone decay; frost not solar stress, and ivy not canopy.

web.text: Acoustic emission tracks solar-driven rock cracking and vegetation is reported to damp rock temperature swings. Whether canopy cuts actual cracking is unproven, and moisture under cover could add other cracking.

why: Strength: clear paired design with a before-after canopy removal; risk: shaded boulders stay wetter, so moisture-driven subcritical cracking may offset the temperature damping, and the 70-95% reduction is likely overstated.
